title: Xen by Neuvana review
description: Auricular tVNS packaged as earbuds — a clever consumer form factor, modest independent evidence.
body:
## Where it leads

Xen by Neuvana takes the most consumer-friendly approach to auricular tVNS in this list. It packages the stimulator as in-ear electrodes built into earbuds, with the parameter playing on top of music from a phone — so a session feels closer to wearing AirPods than wearing a medical device. Modes cover focus, calm and sleep, and intensity is user-controlled. No subscription is required for full operation.

## What are the downsides of Xen by Neuvana?

The evidence base is the weak point. The auricular tVNS mechanism inherits credibility from the broader Parasym/Nurosym literature, but Xen-specific peer-reviewed RCTs do not yet exist; what is published is company-sponsored. The earbud form factor also has a practical downside — in-ear electrode placement is more finicky than a tragus clip, and the device tethers to a control unit by cable.

## Who should buy Xen by Neuvana?

Choose Xen by Neuvana if the earbud form factor and music-paired sessions make daily use realistic for you, and you are comfortable with a thinner device-specific evidence base. If clinical-grade evidence is the priority, Nurosym is the right pick. If you want a wider protocol library at a lower price, Pulsetto delivers more for less.

title: Zoe review
description: The most science-backed CGM programme — and the only one fusing glucose, microbiome and blood biomarkers into one nutrition plan.
body:
## Where it leads

Zoe is the only programme in this list that does not pretend glucose is the whole story. The 2-week CGM phase tracks your [glucose spikes](/glossary/glucose-spikes) alongside a gut [microbiome](/glossary/microbiome) stool test and a blood biomarker panel, and the three signals are fused into a single set of personalised food rankings — backed by the published PREDICT-1 and PREDICT-2 studies from Tim Spector’s King’s College London group. The scientific lineage is the strongest in this category by a meaningful margin.

## What are the downsides of Zoe?

The CGM is a snapshot, not an instrument. Two weeks of Abbott Libre wear feed the initial ranking model and then end; if you want ongoing CGM data, Zoe is the wrong shape. There is no raw data export, the Libre sensor lags Dexcom G7 on accuracy, and the annual subscription commitment after the £300 setup is steep for a programme that has stopped giving you new glucose data after week two.

## Who should buy Zoe?

Choose Zoe if you want personalised nutrition grounded in published science and the once-only CGM phase is enough — it is the right shape for a hard reset of your eating patterns based on your own physiology, not for ongoing glucose tracking. If continuous CGM is the point, Levels (premium) or Stelo (value) are better fits.

title: Best Continuous Glucose Monitors for Biohackers (2026)
description: ONDA ranks the ten best CGMs of 2026 for non-diabetic biohackers — Levels, Nutrisense, Zoe, Stelo, Lingo, Ultrahuman, Signos, Veri, Hello Inside and Supersapiens — scored on insights, accuracy, coaching and value.
body:
## How we ranked them

Every programme was scored against ONDA’s published [review methodology](/reviews/methodology): six weighted criteria, with insights and analysis quality carrying the most weight because that is the category’s real differentiator. Eight of the ten programmes ship the same two underlying sensors — so sensor accuracy alone does not separate them.

All ten programmes were assessed from manufacturer documentation, the published Dexcom G7 and Abbott Libre 3 validation literature, and independent 2026 reviews rather than hands-on testing, so treat the scores as an evidence-based starting point.

## Best Continuous Glucose Monitors for Biohackers: which should you buy?

The market is hardware-converged and software-divergent. Two sensors carry the entire non-diabetic CGM category in 2026: **Abbott Libre 3** (Lingo, Ultrahuman M1, Veri, Hello Inside, Zoe, Supersapiens) and **Dexcom G7** (Levels, Stelo, Nutrisense, Signos). The wrappers are what you are actually buying.

Two clean breakpoints in the price ladder:

**Premium coaching tier ($140–$310/month):** Levels, Nutrisense, Signos. Deepest insights, best app design, most expensive. Right pick if CGM is a serious tool, not an experiment.

**OTC value tier ($22–$100/month):** Lingo, Stelo. No prescription, no subscription required. Same underlying sensors, simpler apps. Right pick if you want to find out whether CGM changes anything for you before committing.

Around those two breakpoints the rest of the field carves out specific use cases — Zoe for multi-biomarker personalisation, Ultrahuman M1 for ring-ecosystem integration, Veri and Hello Inside for EU users, Supersapiens for endurance athletes. The category is small enough that the ten programmes here are effectively the universe; the right answer is which use case fits you.

body:
## How we ranked them

title: Best HRV Trackers (2026)
description: ONDA ranks the best HRV trackers of 2026 — rings, bands, smartwatches and chest straps — scored on measurement accuracy, sleep, data access and value.
body:
## How we ranked them

Every device was scored against ONDA's published [review methodology](/reviews/methodology): seven weighted criteria, with HRV measurement accuracy carrying the most weight because it is the metric this category exists to serve. The overall score is the weighted mean — not a number picked by feel.

All of them were assessed from manufacturer specifications, independent 2026 reviews and published validation literature rather than hands-on testing, so treat the scores as an evidence-based starting point. That literature is consistent: across nocturnal HR and HRV, the Oura Ring (Gen 3/4) shows the strongest agreement with reference measurement, ahead of Whoop, Garmin and Polar's wrist devices — which is why the overnight rings lead this ranking on accuracy. One caveat worth reading first: no two devices report the same HRV number — [here is why your HRV is different on every device](/articles/hrv-different-every-device), and which reading to actually trust.

## Best HRV Trackers: which should you buy?

The scores cluster tightly — every device here is genuinely capable, and the right pick is mostly about how you want to wear it and whether you'll pay a subscription. The Oura Ring 5 wins overall because it does the core job, overnight HRV and sleep, better than anything else you can wear around the clock — for a membership. The big shift in 2026 is the subscription-free field: the RingConn Gen 3, Ultrahuman Ring Pro, RingConn Gen 2 and Amazfit Helio Ring are all strong one-time buys. The Polar H10 would top a pure-accuracy ranking, but a chest strap is a deliberate instrument, not a lifestyle wearable. From there it splits by need: Whoop for athletes, Samsung for Android, Garmin and Apple for an all-day do-everything device, Withings for a discreet ECG watch — and the Circular Ring 2 only if you want its unique ECG/AFib hardware and accept that the software is unfinished. description: ONDA ranks the ten best vagus nerve stimulators of 2026 — auricular tVNS, cervical tVNS, vibrotactile, infrasonic and one implanted reference. Scored on evidence, mechanism, protocols and value.
body:
## How we ranked them

## Best Vagus Nerve Stimulators: which should you buy?

The field splits cleanly into four mechanism classes, and the right pick depends mostly on what you want the stimulation to do.

**Electrical auricular tVNS (ear clip):** Nurosym, Vagustim, Xen by Neuvana. The deepest research base on the consumer side belongs to Nurosym; Vagustim is the protocol-rich EU alternative; Xen is the familiar form factor.

**Electrical cervical tVNS (neck or handheld):** gammaCore Sapphire CV (prescription, FDA-cleared, headache-indicated), Truvaga 350 (consumer, same hardware platform), Pulsetto (consumer collar, broad protocol library), Hoolest VeRelief Prime (handheld, athletic recovery).

**Vibrotactile / mechanical:** Apollo Neuro (wrist/ankle band, daily wear), Sensate (chest pebble, infrasonic, paired with soundscapes). Not electrical tVNS in the strict sense; both have peer-reviewed HRV evidence.

**Implanted:** LivaNova VNS Therapy. The medical gold standard, included as reference rather than recommendation.

If the deciding criterion is evidence, choose Nurosym. If it is daily wearability, Apollo Neuro. If you need prescribed clinical use, gammaCore. If price is the constraint, Pulsetto. The category is small, the differentiation is real, and the scoring above maps directly onto which trade-off matters to you.

title: HRV Biofeedback on Apple Watch: How It Works
description: HRV biofeedback on Apple Watch: what the Watch measures, why it records HRV rather than giving live biofeedback on its own, how accurate it is, and how ONDA turns it into a real-time coherence loop.
body:
HRV biofeedback on Apple Watch: what the Watch measures, why it records HRV rather than giving live biofeedback on its own, how accurate it is, and how ONDA turns it into a real-time coherence loop.

Can the Apple Watch do HRV biofeedback?
The Apple Watch measures heart rate and HRV, but on its own it records HRV as periodic readings rather than giving real-time biofeedback while you breathe. The Watch supplies the heart data; an app like ONDA turns it into a live HRV-biofeedback loop with a coherence score you train against.

Does the Apple Watch measure HRV in real time?
The Watch samples heart rate continuously and logs HRV values, but Apple’s own Health app shows HRV as occasional readings, not a continuous live number. For real-time feedback during a breathing session, you need an app that reads the Watch’s heart data live — such as ONDA.

How accurate is Apple Watch HRV?
The Apple Watch’s optical sensor gives good HRV for tracking trends and recovery, and is well-suited to at-rest readings. It isn’t reference-grade like an ECG chest strap, but for everyday HRV biofeedback and trend tracking it’s more than capable.

Do I need an Apple Watch for HRV biofeedback with ONDA?
No. ONDA also works with the iPhone camera (photoplethysmography) for a resting pulse and breathing reading; HRV and the coherence score need an Apple Watch, which adds continuous heart data and live feedback, but it isn’t required to start.

Is Apple Watch HRV biofeedback a medical tool?
No. HRV biofeedback with the Apple Watch is a self-regulation practice, not a diagnostic or medical device. The Watch’s ECG/AFib features are separate, Apple-cleared functions; HRV biofeedback is about training your breathing and nervous system.

Which biofeedback apps work with the Apple Watch?
Apps that use the Apple Watch's live pulse for real-time HRV or coherence feedback include ONDA — which turns the Watch into a live biofeedback coach with a coherence score inside a guided practice — alongside measurement-first options like Elite HRV and HRV4Training. Apple's built-in Mindfulness and Vitals mostly record rather than feed back live.

Is there a real-time HRV biofeedback app for Apple Watch?
Yes. ONDA uses the Apple Watch's continuous pulse to show your heart rhythm organise into a live coherence score as you breathe, so the Watch becomes a biofeedback coach rather than a passive tracker. You don't need a chest strap — the Watch supplies the signal that unlocks the live coherence score. It is a self-regulation practice, not a medical device.

title: HRV Biofeedback: What It Is, How It Works, and How ONDA Uses It
description: HRV biofeedback explained: what it is, how the real-time feedback loop works, what the evidence supports, how it differs from HRV tracking, and how ONDA implements it. Honest and cited.
body:
HRV biofeedback explained: what it is, how the real-time feedback loop works, what the evidence supports, how it differs from HRV tracking, and how ONDA implements it. Honest and cited.

What is HRV biofeedback?
HRV biofeedback is a technique in which you see your heart-rate variability in real time and adjust your breathing in response — usually breathing slowly at your resonance frequency. The live feedback closes a loop that trains the autonomic nervous system, rather than just recording it.

Does HRV biofeedback actually work?
The acute effect is well established: paced breathing at resonance frequency raises HRV during the session and engages the parasympathetic system. Longer-term benefits for stress and self-regulation are supported but vary between people. It is one of the most evidence-grounded, low-risk self-regulation techniques available.

What is the difference between HRV biofeedback and HRV tracking?
HRV tracking passively records your HRV (often overnight) so you can watch trends — what rings and bands do. HRV biofeedback is active: you get live feedback while you breathe and train your heart rhythm in the moment. Tracking tells you how you recovered; biofeedback gives you something to do about it.

Do I need a chest strap for HRV biofeedback?
Not always. A chest strap gives the most accurate signal, but apps like ONDA use the iPhone camera (photoplethysmography) or an Apple Watch to give usable real-time feedback with no extra hardware.

How long does HRV biofeedback take to work?
You feel the acute effect immediately — HRV rises within a single session. Changes in your resting baseline, where they happen, tend to show over weeks of consistent practice rather than days, and the size of the change varies between people.

Is ONDA HRV biofeedback?
Yes. ONDA is an HRV biofeedback and guided-breathing app: it shows your heart-rhythm response as you breathe, using the iPhone camera or an Apple Watch — with a live coherence score on Apple Watch — inside a guided practice. It is not a medical device.

Is there an app with real-time HRV biofeedback?
Yes. Real-time HRV biofeedback apps show your heart rhythm respond live as you breathe, rather than just logging HRV overnight. ONDA does this from the iPhone camera or an Apple Watch — a live coherence score with an Apple Watch — with no chest strap and inside a guided practice. Elite HRV and HRV4Training also offer live HRV feedback, more as measurement tools.

What is the best real-time HRV biofeedback app?
It depends on the job. For an accessible, guided real-time biofeedback practice with no extra hardware, ONDA leads; for measurement precision with a breathing pacer, Elite HRV (best with a chest strap); for a science-validated daily reading with breathing, HRV4Training. The honest trade-offs are laid out in the ranked guide to apps combining breathing, HRV and real-time feedback.

title: HRV vs Coherence: What’s the Difference?
description: HRV vs coherence explained: HRV is the raw variation between heartbeats; coherence is how smooth and rhythmic that variation is as you breathe. Which to watch, and how ONDA uses each.
body:
HRV vs coherence explained: HRV is the raw variation between heartbeats; coherence is how smooth and rhythmic that variation is as you breathe. Which to watch, and how ONDA uses each.

What is the difference between HRV and coherence?
HRV (heart-rate variability) is the raw variation in time between heartbeats — a measured signal. Coherence describes how smooth, regular and rhythmic that variation is, especially as it lines up with your breathing. HRV is the number; coherence is a measure of the pattern’s quality in the moment.

Is a high coherence score the same as high HRV?
They’re related but not identical. When you breathe at your resonance frequency, HRV rises and the heart rhythm becomes smooth and wave-like — high coherence. But HRV can be high in a noisy, irregular way too (e.g. from arrhythmia). Coherence specifically rewards a clean, organised oscillation, not just raw variability.

Which should I pay attention to?
For in-the-moment breathing practice, coherence is the useful live guide — it shows whether you’re organising your heart rhythm right now. For long-term recovery and adaptation, your resting-HRV trend over weeks is the signal to watch. They answer different questions.

Is coherence a medical or scientific measurement?
No. HRV is a well-defined physiological measure (e.g. RMSSD, SDNN). A coherence score is a derived practice metric — useful real-time feedback, but not a clinical biomarker and not standardised across apps.

How does ONDA use HRV and coherence?
ONDA reads your heartbeat (iPhone camera or Apple Watch) and — with an Apple Watch — shows a live coherence score during practice so you can see your rhythm organise as you breathe. Over time it tracks your resting-HRV trend. Coherence guides the session; the HRV trend tracks progress.

title: Resonance Breathing: The Science Behind Slow Breathing and HRV
description: Resonance breathing explained: what it is, why ~6 breaths a minute maximises HRV, how to find your resonance frequency, the evidence, how to practise, and how ONDA guides it.
body:
Resonance breathing explained: what it is, why ~6 breaths a minute maximises HRV, how to find your resonance frequency, the evidence, how to practise, and how ONDA guides it.

What is resonance breathing?
Resonance breathing (also called coherent breathing) is slow, even breathing at the pace where your heart-rate oscillation is largest — for most people around 5.5–6 breaths a minute, roughly a 10-second cycle. At that pace the heart rhythm and breathing synchronise and HRV rises.

What is my resonance frequency?
Most people’s resonance frequency sits between about 4.5 and 7 breaths a minute, commonly near 6. You can find yours by trying paces in that range and noticing where your breathing feels smoothest and, with a biofeedback app, where HRV peaks.

Does slow breathing really raise HRV?
Yes — breathing near your resonance frequency reliably increases heart-rate variability during the session and engages the parasympathetic branch. It is the core mechanism behind HRV biofeedback. How much your resting baseline changes over time varies between people.

How long should I practise resonance breathing?
A typical session is about 10–20 minutes, but even a few minutes shifts your state. Consistency matters more than length — short daily sessions tend to help more than occasional long ones.

Is resonance breathing the same as box breathing?
No. Box breathing uses equal counts with holds (e.g. 4-4-4-4). Resonance breathing is smooth, continuous breathing without holds at a specific slow pace (~6/min) chosen to maximise heart-rate oscillation. Both calm you; resonance breathing is the one tied to HRV.

title: HR Acceleration: Average Beat-to-Beat Change
description: HR Acceleration here is a small number that describes whether your beat-to-beat intervals were, on average, getting longer or shorter from one beat to the next during the last 15 seconds. Despite its name, it is a…
body:
What this number shows
HR Acceleration here is a small number that describes whether your beat-to-beat intervals were, on average, getting longer or shorter from one beat to the next during the last 15 seconds. Despite its name, it is a simple average of successive differences, not a true second derivative of heart rate.
How this tool calculates it
The tool takes the differences between consecutive RR intervals (in ms), averages them (skipping the first one), and divides by 100. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.
How to read it
Positive: RR intervals were getting longer on average, which means heart rate was drifting down during the window. This often happens during a slow exhale or as you settle.
Negative: RR intervals were getting shorter, so heart rate was drifting up, for example on an inhale, after moving, or as you get tense.
Near zero: No clear drift. This is the most common value at rest, because the natural speed-up and slow-down with each breath cancels out.
Why it jumps around
Your heart naturally speeds up a little when you breathe in and slows when you breathe out (respiratory sinus arrhythmia). Over a 15-second window that contains only two or three breaths, where the window starts and ends in the breathing cycle strongly affects this value. Camera timing errors of a few milliseconds per beat add more noise. Small values in either direction are best read as "no meaningful change".
Important limits
This is not a standard clinical or sports-science metric, and there are no established normal ranges for it. It is shown as a quick directional indicator only, not as a medical or fitness measurement.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.
Positive means beats were spreading out (pulse slowing); negative means they were bunching up (pulse rising).

title: Alarm / Anxiety: An Experimental Index
description: Alarm here is an experimental index built from rhythm irregularity and breathing rate. It is not an anxiety test and it cannot detect fear or worry. It rises when your beat-to-beat intervals look irregular relative…
body:
What this number is
Alarm here is an experimental index built from rhythm irregularity and breathing rate. It is not an anxiety test and it cannot detect fear or worry. It rises when your beat-to-beat intervals look irregular relative to their average (high CSI) and when your estimated breathing rate is above 15 breaths per minute.
How this tool calculates it
Alarm = 0.7 × Stress + 3 × (breathing rate − 15, if above 15), limited to 0–100%. Stress = 130 × CSI. Heart rate itself is not part of this formula. Breathing rate is estimated from slow swings in the pulse signal and counts as 0 when no clear rhythm is found. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.
How to read it
Higher: Beat intervals varied a lot relative to their mean and/or breathing was estimated above 15 per minute. Talking, moving your finger, cold fingers or dim light can raise it as much as a stressful moment can.
Lower: The rhythm looked steady and breathing was estimated at 15 per minute or slower.
Important limits
This is an experimental heuristic built from a few camera-derived inputs. It is not a validated physiological measure, it is not emotion detection, and it is not a medical test. Treat it as a rough hint about the direction your signal is moving, not as a verdict about how you feel. If you feel anxious or unwell, trust that feeling over this number and seek appropriate help. A low score does not mean you are fine, and a high score does not mean something is wrong.
What actually helps
Longer exhales: Breathing in for about 4 seconds and out for about 6 is a simple way to slow down when you feel keyed up.
Re-measure calmly: Sit, rest your arm on a table, keep your finger still, and measure again after a minute. Many high readings are signal noise.
Physiological sigh: Two short inhales through the nose followed by a long exhale is another quick, low-effort way to settle.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.
Alarm reacts to an irregular-looking rhythm and faster breathing. Check the signal and your surroundings before reading anything into it.

title: BPM: Your Heart Rate and What Changes It
description: Heart rate is the number of heartbeats per minute (bpm). It rises when your body needs more blood flow, for example during movement, heat, stress, illness or after caffeine, and falls during rest and sleep. Resting…
body:
What heart rate is
Heart rate is the number of heartbeats per minute (bpm). It rises when your body needs more blood flow, for example during movement, heat, stress, illness or after caffeine, and falls during rest and sleep. Resting heart rate is a useful everyday health marker when you track it over time.
How this tool calculates it
Your fingertip over the camera changes color slightly with each pulse (photoplethysmography, PPG). The tool finds each pulse peak in the red channel, measures the time between peaks (RR intervals), drops implausible ones, and computes heart rate as 60,000 divided by the average interval in milliseconds. Results outside 40–180 bpm are discarded. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.
Typical ranges
About 60–100 bpm: The commonly cited normal resting range for adults. Many healthy people, especially active ones, rest lower.
Below 60 bpm: Often normal in fit people and during deep rest; see a doctor if it comes with dizziness, fainting or unusual tiredness.
Above 100 bpm at rest: Can follow caffeine, stress, dehydration or illness. If it stays high at rest or comes with chest pain or breathlessness, seek medical advice.
How accurate is a camera reading?
Camera heart rate is usually close to a reference device when you hold still in good light, but it is less reliable with movement, cold fingers, heavy pressure or dim lighting. It is an educational estimate, not a medical measurement.
Practical tips
Measure resting HR consistently: For example sitting quietly for a minute after waking, before coffee.
Slow breathing: A few minutes of slow breathing with a longer exhale often lowers heart rate a little.
Long-term habits: Regular aerobic exercise, good sleep and limited alcohol tend to lower resting heart rate over weeks.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.
Heart rate is easiest to learn from when you measure it the same way each time and look at the trend.

title: Breathing Rate: Breaths per Minute Explained
description: Breathing (respiratory) rate is the number of breaths you take per minute. It is one of the basic vital signs, and it is also the one you can change most easily on purpose, which is why slow breathing is used in many…
body:
What breathing rate is
Breathing (respiratory) rate is the number of breaths you take per minute. It is one of the basic vital signs, and it is also the one you can change most easily on purpose, which is why slow breathing is used in many relaxation methods.
How this tool calculates it
Breathing slightly changes the strength of each pulse wave in your fingertip. The tool smooths the size of the pulse signal over about 5 seconds, finds the peaks of that slow wave (at least 2 seconds apart), takes the median time between them and converts it to breaths per minute. It shows a value only when it finds at least five such peaks and the result is between 6 and 30 breaths per minute; otherwise it shows nothing. Because the window is short and the effect is subtle, this is an approximate estimate.
Typical ranges
About 12–20 per minute: The usual resting range for adults.
Slower (about 6–10): Common during deliberate slow breathing, meditation or deep rest.
Faster (above about 20 at rest): Can come with exertion, anxiety, fever or illness. Persistently fast breathing at rest, or breathlessness, is worth checking with a doctor.
Why slow breathing is popular
Breathing slowly, often around 5–7 breaths per minute with a relaxed, longer exhale, tends to increase the heart-rate swings that follow each breath and is associated with feeling calmer. It is a low-risk, well-studied technique. If you feel lightheaded, return to normal breathing.
Tips for a better reading
Rest your hand, keep the finger still with light pressure, breathe naturally, and give the tool at least 20–30 seconds. Talking or moving makes the estimate unreliable.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.
Breathing rate here is estimated from the slow rise and fall of your pulse signal; treat it as approximate.

title: CSI: Cardiac Stability Index Explained
description: CSI in this tool is the coefficient of variation of your beat-to-beat intervals: how much the intervals vary compared with their average length. Because it is divided by the mean interval, it lets you compare rhythm…
body:
What this number shows
CSI in this tool is the coefficient of variation of your beat-to-beat intervals: how much the intervals vary compared with their average length. Because it is divided by the mean interval, it lets you compare rhythm evenness at different heart rates. Lower means the intervals were more alike; higher means more variation.
How this tool calculates it
CSI = standard deviation of the RR intervals ÷ mean RR interval. For example, if your intervals average 800 ms with a standard deviation of 40 ms, CSI is 0.05. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.
Why camera values look high
With a phone camera, beat timing is only accurate to a few milliseconds and some peaks are misplaced, so the measured spread is larger than the true one. In practice readings around 0.3 are typical on this page; lower values mean a cleaner, steadier signal.
Lower (well under 0.3): Intervals were fairly even and the signal was clean.
Around 0.3: A typical camera reading.
Clearly higher: Intervals varied a lot: often movement, pressing too hard, cold fingers or poor light; occasionally genuinely irregular beats.
CSI and heart rate variability
Some variation between beats is healthy: the heart speeds up slightly on each inhale and slows on each exhale, and people with good fitness often show more of this at rest. So lower is not automatically "better" in physiology. In this tool, however, CSI is mainly a check on how steady and clean the reading was, and it feeds the Stress (130 × CSI), Energy, Relaxation and Alarm indices.
Health note
If you notice a persistently irregular pulse, palpitations, dizziness or shortness of breath, see a doctor. A browser camera reading cannot detect or rule out arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.
CSI is the spread of your beat intervals divided by their average; typical camera readings sit around 0.3.

title: Energy %: An Experimental Heart-Rate Index
description: Energy here is an experimental index, not a measure of how energetic you feel, your fitness, or a "battery". It starts at 90% and goes down when your heart rate is above 75 bpm and when your beat-to-beat rhythm is…
body:
What this number is
Energy here is an experimental index, not a measure of how energetic you feel, your fitness, or a "battery". It starts at 90% and goes down when your heart rate is above 75 bpm and when your beat-to-beat rhythm is irregular relative to its average (CSI).
How this tool calculates it
Energy = 90 − 1.5 × (heart rate − 75, if above 75) − 80 × CSI, limited to 10–100%. For example, at 70 bpm with a typical camera CSI of 0.3, Energy is about 66%; at 95 bpm with the same CSI, it is about 36%. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.
How to read it
Higher: Your pulse was at or below about 75 bpm and the rhythm looked steady.
Lower: A faster pulse (coffee, movement, heat, stress, illness) and/or an irregular-looking rhythm, which is often just a noisy signal.
Important limits
This is an experimental heuristic built from a few camera-derived inputs. It is not a validated physiological measure, it is not emotion detection, and it is not a medical test. Treat it as a rough hint about the direction your signal is moving, not as a verdict about how you feel. Because of the formula, Energy cannot exceed 90% and a resting pulse below 75 bpm is not rewarded any further.
What actually helps
Sleep: Consistent, sufficient sleep is the strongest lever for daytime energy.
Movement and daylight: A short walk, especially outdoors in the morning, often helps more than extra caffeine.
Short resets: A few minutes of slow breathing can lower a racing pulse and help you feel more settled.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.
Energy here drops with a pulse above 75 bpm and an irregular-looking rhythm. It is a rough hint, not a fuel gauge.

title: Excitement: An Experimental Arousal Index
description: Excitement here is an experimental index of general physiological arousal. It rises with heart rate above 60 bpm and, a little, with breathing rate. It cannot tell positive excitement apart from nervousness, physical…
body:
What this number is
Excitement here is an experimental index of general physiological arousal. It rises with heart rate above 60 bpm and, a little, with breathing rate. It cannot tell positive excitement apart from nervousness, physical effort or caffeine, because the body shows all of these with a faster pulse.
How this tool calculates it
Excitement = 1.5 × (heart rate − 60) + 0.5 × breathing rate, limited to 0–100%. Heart rate is 60,000 divided by the average RR interval; breathing rate is estimated from slow changes in the pulse signal and counts as 0 when the tool cannot find a clear rhythm. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.
How to read it
Higher: Your heart rate was well above 60 bpm. At 80 bpm and 15 breaths per minute, for example, the index is about 38%; at 100 bpm it is about 68%.
Lower: Your pulse was close to 60 bpm or below. Many relaxed, fit adults sit here at rest.
Important limits
This is an experimental heuristic built from a few camera-derived inputs. It is not a validated physiological measure, it is not emotion detection, and it is not a medical test. Treat it as a rough hint about the direction your signal is moving, not as a verdict about how you feel. In practice this index is mostly a rescaled heart rate, so it carries the same caveats as heart rate itself.
What actually helps
Name the cause: If the number is high, ask what just happened: movement, coffee, a stressful message, or anticipation. The body response is similar in each case.
Slow exhale to settle: If you want to calm down, a few breaths with a longer exhale than inhale tend to lower heart rate over a minute or two.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.
Excitement is essentially "how far above 60 bpm is your pulse right now", expressed as a percentage.

title: Fatigue: An Experimental Energy/Stress Index
description: Fatigue on this page is an experimental index. It is not a measure of sleepiness, muscle fatigue or overtraining. It is computed from two other indices in the tool, Energy and Stress, so it rises when your heart rate…
body:
What this number is
Fatigue on this page is an experimental index. It is not a measure of sleepiness, muscle fatigue or overtraining. It is computed from two other indices in the tool, Energy and Stress, so it rises when your heart rate is above about 75 bpm and when your beat-to-beat rhythm looks irregular.
How this tool calculates it
Fatigue = 60 × (1 − Energy/100) + 0.2 × Stress, limited to 0–100%. Energy falls as heart rate climbs above 75 bpm and as CSI (the irregularity of your beat intervals) rises; Stress is CSI × 130. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.
How to read it
Higher: Your pulse was elevated and/or your beat intervals varied a lot relative to their average. Being tired can do this, but so can coffee, having just climbed stairs, talking, or a noisy camera signal.
Lower: Heart rate was moderate and the rhythm looked steady during the reading.
Important limits
This is an experimental heuristic built from a few camera-derived inputs. It is not a validated physiological measure, it is not emotion detection, and it is not a medical test. Treat it as a rough hint about the direction your signal is moving, not as a verdict about how you feel. Real fatigue assessment usually looks at trends over days (resting heart rate, HRV measured the same way each morning, sleep), not a single short reading.
What actually helps
Consistent sleep: Regular bed and wake times are one of the most dependable ways to feel less worn out.
Track trends, not moments: If you want to monitor recovery, measure at the same time each day, sitting still, and look at the week rather than one number.
Easy movement and breaks: A short walk or a few minutes of slow breathing can help you reset during a long day.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.
A high Fatigue value is a prompt to check the basics (sleep, caffeine, recent activity), not a diagnosis.

title: Flow: An Experimental Focus + Relaxation Index
description: Flow here is an experimental index that tries to capture a combination people often describe during absorbed work: attention that holds steady while the body stays reasonably calm. The browser tool cannot read your…
body:
What this number is
Flow here is an experimental index that tries to capture a combination people often describe during absorbed work: attention that holds steady while the body stays reasonably calm. The browser tool cannot read your attention or your mind. It only combines two of its other indices, Focus and Relaxation, which themselves come from your heart rate and the irregularity of your beat-to-beat intervals.
How this tool calculates it
Flow = 0.6 × Focus + 0.4 × Relaxation, limited to 0–100%. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually. Because Focus and Relaxation both rise when your heart rate is moderate and your rhythm is steady (low CSI), Flow rises in the same situations.
How to read it
Higher: Your pulse was moderate and your beat intervals were fairly even during the reading. That can accompany calm, engaged attention, but it can also simply mean you sat still with a clean signal.
Lower: Heart rate was higher, the rhythm looked more irregular, or both. Movement, finger pressure changes and poor lighting push it down too, because they add noise to the camera signal.
Important limits
This is an experimental heuristic built from a few camera-derived inputs. It is not a validated physiological measure, it is not emotion detection, and it is not a medical test. Treat it as a rough hint about the direction your signal is moving, not as a verdict about how you feel. The psychological state called "flow" is studied with questionnaires and task performance, and there is no accepted way to detect it from a 15-second fingertip reading.
What actually helps
Reduce interruptions: Close notifications and pick one task. Frequent switching is a reliable way to break concentration.
Slow breathing before deep work: A few minutes of slow, relaxed breathing often lowers heart rate a little and makes the rhythm steadier.
Sleep and breaks: Attention is easier to sustain when you are rested; short breaks every hour or so help too.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.
Use Flow as a curiosity, not a score to chase: it goes up when your pulse is moderate and your rhythm is steady.

title: Focus / Concentration: An Experimental Index
description: Focus here is an experimental index. It does not measure attention, and a camera on your fingertip cannot know what you are thinking about. It averages two other indices in the tool, Energy and inverse Stress, so it…
body:
What this number is
Focus here is an experimental index. It does not measure attention, and a camera on your fingertip cannot know what you are thinking about. It averages two other indices in the tool, Energy and inverse Stress, so it is highest when your heart rate is moderate (at or below about 75 bpm) and your beat-to-beat rhythm is steady.
How this tool calculates it
Focus = 0.5 × Energy + 0.5 × (100 − Stress), limited to 0–100%. Energy = 90 − 1.5 × (heart rate above 75 bpm) − 80 × CSI; Stress = 130 × CSI, where CSI is the standard deviation of your RR intervals divided by their mean. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.
How to read it
Higher: Moderate pulse and even beat intervals during the reading. This can go along with calm, steady work, but a relaxed person reading nothing at all will score the same.
Lower: A faster pulse, a more irregular rhythm, or a noisy signal from finger movement.
Important limits
This is an experimental heuristic built from a few camera-derived inputs. It is not a validated physiological measure, it is not emotion detection, and it is not a medical test. Treat it as a rough hint about the direction your signal is moving, not as a verdict about how you feel. Heart signals change with concentration in lab studies, but not in a way that lets a short camera reading tell you how focused you are.
What actually helps
One task at a time: Set a clear goal for the next 25–50 minutes and remove obvious distractions.
Calm body first: Slow breathing for a few minutes before demanding work can lower arousal if you feel wired.
Rest: Sleep, hydration and regular breaks do more for concentration than any single number.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.
Focus rises when your pulse is moderate and your rhythm is steady. It is a hint about your body, not a reading of your mind.

title: HRV (RMSSD): Beat-to-Beat Variation Explained
description: Heart rate variability (HRV) is the natural variation in time between heartbeats. A healthy heart does not tick like a metronome: intervals lengthen and shorten with breathing, posture and nervous-system activity.…
body:
What HRV is
Heart rate variability (HRV) is the natural variation in time between heartbeats. A healthy heart does not tick like a metronome: intervals lengthen and shorten with breathing, posture and nervous-system activity. RMSSD, the root mean square of successive differences, is one of the most widely used HRV measures and mainly reflects parasympathetic (vagal) activity, the "rest and digest" side of the nervous system.
How this tool calculates it
The tool takes each pair of consecutive RR intervals, squares their difference, averages those squares and takes the square root, giving a value in milliseconds. Values above 100 ms are capped at 100. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.
Typical ranges and what affects them
Resting RMSSD in healthy adults varies widely, often roughly 20–80 ms, and tends to be higher in younger and fitter people and lower with age. It usually drops after poor sleep, alcohol, illness, intense training or acute stress, and rises with good recovery. Differences between people are large, so your own trend matters more than comparison with others.
Higher than your usual: Often seen when rested and relaxed.
Lower than your usual: Common with fatigue, stress, alcohol, illness or a late heavy meal.
Why camera readings are rough
RMSSD depends on millisecond-level timing. A phone camera at about 30 frames per second, a fingertip that shifts slightly, and a window of only 15 seconds all add error, usually inflating the value. Standard short-term HRV measurements use at least a few minutes of ECG or a chest strap. Treat the number here as a rough estimate and compare readings only when taken the same way.
Practical tips
Measure consistently: For trends, measure at the same time (for example after waking), sitting still, breathing normally.
Slow breathing: Slow breathing at around 6 breaths per minute typically increases beat-to-beat variation while you do it.
Basics first: Regular sleep, limited alcohol and aerobic exercise are associated with higher resting HRV over time.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.
RMSSD reflects vagal activity; the camera version here is a rough estimate, most useful when compared with your own readings.

title: Recovery Rate: How Fast Your Pulse Settles
description: Recovery Rate in this tool is a within-window measure. It looks at the highest heart rate in the last 15 seconds and asks how far the most recent beat has come back from that peak toward the window average. It is not…
body:
What this number shows
Recovery Rate in this tool is a within-window measure. It looks at the highest heart rate in the last 15 seconds and asks how far the most recent beat has come back from that peak toward the window average. It is not the same as the clinical "heart rate recovery" test, which measures how many beats per minute your pulse drops in the first minute after hard exercise.
How this tool calculates it
For each beat the tool converts the RR interval to beats per minute. If the peak is at least 2 bpm above the window average, Recovery = (peak − latest beat) ÷ (peak − average) × 100, limited to 0–100%. If there was no clear peak, the value is 0. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.
How to read it
Near 100%: The latest beat is back at (or below) your average for the window, so any short spike has passed.
Around 50%: Your pulse is about halfway back from its recent peak.
Near 0%: Either your pulse is still at its peak, or there was no noticeable peak at all (a steady reading also shows 0). Check the other numbers to tell these apart.
Why it moves a lot
Heart rate naturally rises on each inhale and falls on each exhale, so the "peak" is often just the top of a breath cycle and the value can swing from beat to beat. A single false or missed beat from the camera can also create an artificial peak.
Recovery in the broader sense
Over hours and days, recovery is better judged by trends: morning resting heart rate, HRV measured the same way each day, sleep, and how you feel. After exercise, a faster drop in heart rate during the first minute is generally a sign of good fitness.
Important limits
This is a rough, experimental indicator of this browser tool, not a medical or training metric.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.
High means your pulse is back near its average after a recent peak; 0% can also simply mean there was no peak.

title: Relaxation / Calmness: An Experimental Index
description: Relaxation here is an experimental index that goes up when your beat-to-beat rhythm looks steady and your Energy index is high (which in this tool mostly means your heart rate is not above about 75 bpm). It is not a…
body:
What this number is
Relaxation here is an experimental index that goes up when your beat-to-beat rhythm looks steady and your Energy index is high (which in this tool mostly means your heart rate is not above about 75 bpm). It is not a measure of how calm you feel, and it is not a validated relaxation score.
How this tool calculates it
Relaxation = 60 × (1 − min(1, 1.5 × CSI)) + 0.2 × Energy, limited to 0–100%. CSI is the standard deviation of your RR intervals divided by their mean. Note that breathing rate is not part of this formula, even though slow breathing often does help you relax. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.
How to read it
Higher: Your RR intervals varied little relative to their average, and your pulse was moderate. Sitting still with a clean signal pushes it up.
Lower: The rhythm looked more irregular (higher CSI) or your pulse was faster. Finger movement also adds irregularity and lowers the score.
Important limits
This is an experimental heuristic built from a few camera-derived inputs. It is not a validated physiological measure, it is not emotion detection, and it is not a medical test. Treat it as a rough hint about the direction your signal is moving, not as a verdict about how you feel. One quirk: in real physiology, a relaxed body often shows more beat-to-beat variation linked to breathing, while this index rewards less variation. That is one more reason to treat it as a rough hint only.
What actually helps
Slow breathing: Breathing slowly, around 5–7 breaths per minute with a relaxed longer exhale, is a well-studied way to calm the body for most people.
Posture and stillness: Sit comfortably, drop your shoulders and rest your hand so the finger stays on the lens without pressing hard.
A few quiet minutes: Heart rate usually settles over several minutes of rest, not seconds.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.
Relaxation here mostly reflects a moderate pulse and a steady-looking rhythm. How you feel matters more than the number.

title: HR Trend Slope: Is Your Pulse Rising or Falling?
description: The HR trend slope tells you whether your heart rate was drifting up or down across the current measurement window. It is useful for watching a change happen in real time, such as your pulse settling as you breathe…
body:
What this number shows
The HR trend slope tells you whether your heart rate was drifting up or down across the current measurement window. It is useful for watching a change happen in real time, such as your pulse settling as you breathe slowly or climbing after you stand up.
How this tool calculates it
The tool fits a straight line (linear regression) through your RR intervals in order, beat by beat. It then flips the sign and divides by 100, so that a positive value means heart rate is rising (intervals getting shorter) and a negative value means heart rate is falling (intervals getting longer). The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.
How to read it
Positive: Your pulse was trending upward during the window: for example after moving, talking, standing, or during tension.
Negative: Your pulse was trending downward: common when you sit down, relax, or breathe slowly with longer exhales.
Close to zero: Heart rate was roughly flat. At steady rest this is what you would expect.
Why it can be noisy
Within 15 seconds your heart rate naturally rises and falls with each breath, so the fitted line can tilt one way or the other just because of where the window starts. Camera-based beat timing also has small errors. Look for a consistent sign over half a minute or more rather than reacting to a single value.
A simple experiment
Sit still, let the reading settle, then breathe slowly: about 4 seconds in and 6 seconds out for a minute. Many people see the slope move toward negative values as their pulse eases down. Then stand up and watch it turn positive as heart rate briefly rises.
Important limits
This is a real-time trend indicator for this browser tool. It has no standard normal range and is not a medical measurement.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.
Positive means your pulse is climbing; negative means it is easing down.

title: Stress %: An Experimental Irregularity Index
description: Stress on this page is an experimental index. It is simply the Cardiac Stability Index (CSI), the variation of your beat-to-beat intervals relative to their average, rescaled to a percentage. It does not measure…
body:
What this number is
Stress on this page is an experimental index. It is simply the Cardiac Stability Index (CSI), the variation of your beat-to-beat intervals relative to their average, rescaled to a percentage. It does not measure stress hormones, emotions or how stressed you feel, and it is not a validated stress score.
How this tool calculates it
Stress = 130 × CSI, limited to 0–100%. A typical camera CSI of about 0.3 gives roughly 40%. Heart rate and breathing rate are not part of this formula. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.
How to read it
Higher: Your beat intervals varied more relative to their mean. That can accompany tension, but the most common cause on a phone camera is signal noise: moving your finger, pressing too hard, cold hands or weak light.
Lower: The intervals were more even and the signal was cleaner.
Important limits
This is an experimental heuristic built from a few camera-derived inputs. It is not a validated physiological measure, it is not emotion detection, and it is not a medical test. Treat it as a rough hint about the direction your signal is moving, not as a verdict about how you feel. In real physiology, acute stress usually lowers short-term heart rate variability rather than raising it, so a higher irregularity score is not a reliable stress sign. If stress is affecting your daily life, talking to a professional is more useful than any reading.
What actually helps
Slow breathing with a longer exhale: Several minutes of slow breathing is one of the simplest ways to calm the body.
Better readings: Rest your forearm on a table, cover the camera lightly and hold still for 30 seconds or more before looking at the number.
Daily habits: Sleep, regular exercise, time outdoors and social contact all help with long-term stress.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.
Stress here is 130 × CSI: a rough rhythm-irregularity hint, strongly affected by signal quality.
